title: Redundant assets
objectives: Detect a redundant asset in a payoff matrix from its rank.
Price a redundant asset by replication and spot an arbitrage.

screens.title: Copy the fund
screens.prose: Three assets pay out in one year. Each row is a state of the world, and each column is an asset. Nobody knows which state will happen.

state.caption: Payoffs in £ in one year, one row per state of the world

screens.question: How many units of the bond and of the stock pay exactly what one unit of the fund pays?

hints.text: In the Flat state everything pays 100. Try the Down and Up rows.
In each state the fund pays exactly halfway between the bond and the stock.
$0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times 80 = 90$. Check the Up row the same way.

feedback.correct: Half a bond and half a stock pay 90, 100 and 115.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In each row, bond units times the bond payoff plus stock units times the stock payoff must equal the fund.

byKey.r0c1: Check the Down row: bond units $\times 100$ + stock units $\times 80$ must make 90.
byKey.r1c1: Check the Up row: bond units $\times 100$ + stock units $\times 130$ must make 115.

explain.text: Half a bond plus half a stock pays $50 + 40 = 90$, $50 + 50 = 100$ and $50 + 65 = 115$. That matches the fund in every state. The fund's payoff column is a combination of the other two.

screens.title: Price the copy
screens.prose: Today the bond costs £95 and the stock £100. Half a bond and half a stock pay what the fund pays, in every state.

state.caption: Payoffs in £ in one year, one row per state of the world

screens.question: What must one unit of the fund cost today?

hints.text: What does the copy cost?
You buy half a bond and half a stock.

feedback.correct: The copy costs £97.50, so the fund must too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the copy: half a bond plus half a stock.

byKey.whole: You bought a whole bond and a whole stock. That pays twice the fund, so halve it.
byKey.average: You averaged the fund's payoffs. Today's price comes from what its copy costs, not from the payoffs.

explain.text: The copy costs $0.5 \times 95 + 0.5 \times 100 = \text{£}97.50$. Two things with the same payoff in every state must cost the same. That is the **law of one price**.

screens.title: Redundant
screens.prose: An asset whose payoff column is a combination of the others is **redundant**: you can replicate it. Put the payoffs in a matrix $\mathbf{P}$, one row per state and one column per asset.
screens.question: What is the rank of $\mathbf{P}$?

options.why: Three columns, but the fund's is half the bond's plus half the stock's. Only two are independent.
The bond and stock columns are not multiples of each other: one is flat, the other is not.

hints.text: Rank counts the independent columns.
Column 3 is half of column 1 plus half of column 2.
Columns 1 and 2 are independent, and column 3 adds nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the columns that are not combinations of the others.

explain.text: The bond and the stock are independent, and the fund adds nothing new. So $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{P} = 2$, and the square matrix $\mathbf{P}$ has $\det \mathbf{P} = 0$. Three assets with rank 2 leave one redundant asset.

screens.title: Which can you copy?
screens.prose: Keep the bond, paying 100 in every state, and the stock, paying 80, 100 and 130. Four new assets are offered.
screens.question: Which are redundant given the bond and the stock? Select all that apply.

options.why: A bond-and-stock mix paying 0 when Down and Flat holds none of either. It then pays 0 when Up, not 100.
Matching Down and Flat needs 1.4 bonds and $-0.5$ stock. That pays $140 - 65 = 75$ when Up, not 120.

hints.text: Use Down and Flat to fix the units, then test the Up state.
Geared is 2 stocks minus 1 bond: $160 - 100 = 60$ when Down.
Fund and Geared pass the Up test; Digital and Note fail it.

feedback.correct: Fund and Geared can be copied; Digital and Note cannot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each asset, solve Down and Flat for the units, then check Up.

explain.text: Fund $= \tfrac12$ bond $+ \tfrac12$ stock and Geared $= 2$ stocks $- 1$ bond. Digital and Note each need a new direction. Adding either would raise the rank to 3.

screens.title: A mispriced fund
screens.prose: The fund trades at £99, above its copy at £97.50. You sell 2 funds and buy 1 bond and 1 stock. The table shows the payoffs of each leg.
screens.question: How much cash do you take in today?

hints.text: You receive the price of what you sell and pay the price of what you buy.
Selling 2 funds brings in $2 \times 99 = 198$.

feedback.correct: You keep £3 today and owe nothing later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add what you receive for the funds, then subtract the bond and the stock.

byKey.per-fund: That is the profit per fund. You sold two.
byKey.sign: Selling brings cash in. You receive £198 and pay £195, a gain of £3.

explain.text: You receive $2 \times 99 = \text{£}198$ and pay $95 + 100 = \text{£}195$, so you keep £3. The net payoff is 0 in every state, so nothing can go wrong later. A riskless profit like this is an **arbitrage**.

screens.title: Redundant, not useless
screens.prose: A colleague says the fund is redundant, so it adds nothing and is worth nothing. The bond still costs £95 and the stock £100.

state.caption: Payoffs in £ in one year, one row per state of the world

screens.question: What is the fund's fair price?

options.why: You read redundant as worthless. The fund pays at least £90 in every state. Redundant means it can be copied, so its copy prices it.
The zero determinant says the fund adds no new direction. That is exactly what lets the bond and the stock price it.
That is the quote you just traded against. The copy says £97.50, and the gap was the arbitrage.

hints.text: What does it cost to build the fund's payoff another way?
Half a bond and half a stock pay what the fund pays.

feedback.correct: Redundant means replicable, so the price is the copy's cost, £97.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A redundant asset still pays out. Price it by what its copy costs.

byKey.zero: You read redundant as worthless. The fund still pays £90 to £115. Its copy costs £97.50, so that is its price.

explain.text: Redundant means replicable, not worthless. The fund pays £90 to £115, and its copy costs $0.5 \times 95 + 0.5 \times 100 = \text{£}97.50$. Any other price is an arbitrage.

screens.title: More assets than states
screens.prose: A market has two states, Down and Up, and three assets. The columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ are their payoffs in £.
screens.question: At least how many of the three assets are redundant?

options.why: No column is a multiple of another, but there are only two rows. Three columns in two rows have rank at most 2.
Any two of these columns are independent, so the rank is 2. That leaves $3 - 2 = 1$ redundant.

hints.text: How large can the rank of a matrix with two rows be?
Rank is at most the number of rows: 2.
Three assets minus rank 2 is 1.

feedback.correct: Rank at most 2, so at least one of three assets is redundant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the number of assets with the largest rank possible.

explain.text: A matrix with 2 rows has rank at most 2. Three assets with rank 2 leave $3 - 2 = 1$ redundant. Here $(0, 50) = \tfrac57 (70, 140) - \tfrac12 (100, 100)$.

screens.title: Count them in code
screens.prose: With many assets, let NumPy find the rank. `np.linalg.matrix_rank(P)` returns the rank of `P`. Here `P` has one row per state and one column per asset.
screens.question: Complete `count_redundant(P)` so it returns how many assets are redundant, as an `int`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each must return the exact whole number. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The number of assets is the number of columns.
`P.shape` is (states, assets), so `P.shape[1]` counts the assets.
`n_assets = P.shape[1]` and `rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(P)`.

feedback.correct: Assets minus rank counts the redundant ones.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Count columns, not rows, and use `np.linalg.matrix_rank`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that both `...` lines are replaced.

explain.text:
Columns are assets, so `P.shape[1]` counts them. Each independent column adds one to the rank; every other column is redundant.

```python
n_assets = P.shape[1]
rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(P)
```

screens.prose: You counted directions, not assets: $$\text{redundant assets} = \text{assets} - \operatorname{rank} \mathbf{P}$$ Each redundant asset is priced by its copy. With as many assets as states, $\det \mathbf{P} \ne 0$ means none is redundant and every payoff can be built. Such a market is **complete**.
screens.question: Four states, five assets, and $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{P} = 4$. How many assets are redundant?

options.why: The rank is as large as 4 rows allow, but there are 5 assets. One must be a combination of the others.
4 is the rank: the number of independent assets. The redundant count is $5 - 4$.

hints.text: Subtract the rank from the number of assets.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redundant assets are the assets beyond the rank.

explain.text: Rank 4 means four independent payoff columns. The fifth asset is a combination of them, so $5 - 4 = 1$ asset is redundant. This market is also complete: four independent payoffs span all four states.

screens.title: Why the copy sets the price
screens.prose: Write $\mathbf{c}_1$, $\mathbf{c}_2$ and $\mathbf{c}_3$ for the payoff columns of the bond, the stock and the fund. Write $\pi_1$, $\pi_2$ and $\pi_3$ for their prices today.
screens.question: Put the steps of the argument in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{c}_3 = \tfrac12 \mathbf{c}_1 + \tfrac12 \mathbf{c}_2$, the fund's column is a combination
So half a bond and half a stock pay $\mathbf{c}_3$, state by state
Same payoff in every state means same price today, by the law of one price
$\pi_3 = \tfrac12 \pi_1 + \tfrac12 \pi_2 = \text{£}97.50$, the prices combine like the payoffs

hints.text: Start from the payoff columns.
The portfolio comes next, then the principle that links payoffs to prices.
Columns, portfolio, law of one price, then the number.

feedback.correct: Payoffs combine, so prices combine with the same weights.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the columns and end with the price.

explain.text: The weights that build the payoff also build the price: $\pi_3 = \tfrac12(95) + \tfrac12(100) = \text{£}97.50$. This holds for any redundant asset, whatever its weights.

screens.title: A put from a call
screens.prose: A stock trades at £100. In three months it ends at £80, £100 or £120. A call with strike £100 costs £8.50. A bond paying £100 in three months costs £99.00.

state.caption: Payoffs in £ at expiry; the put and the call both have strike £100

screens.question: Replicate the put with calls, stocks and bonds, then price it.

hints.text: The put pays 20 only in the £80 state. Start from the bond and subtract the stock.
Bond minus stock pays $20, 0, -20$. A call adds back 20 in the top state.
1 call, $-1$ stock, 1 bond. Price: $8.50 - 100 + 99.00$.

feedback.correct: Put = call − stock + bond, so it costs £7.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the put's payoff in each state, then price the holdings.

byKey.r0c1: Without a call, bond minus stock pays $-20$ when the stock ends at £120. One call adds 20 there.
byKey.r1c1: You need to be short one stock: bond minus stock pays $100 - 80 = 20$ in the low state.
byKey.r2c1: One bond supplies the £100 strike in every state.

explain.text: Call minus stock plus bond pays $(20, 0, 0)$, so the put's column adds nothing to the rank: the put is redundant. It costs $8.50 - 100 + 99.00 = \text{£}7.50$. This is **put-call parity**, true in every state since $\max(K - S, 0) = \max(S - K, 0) - S + K$.

ideas: A payoff matrix has one row per state and one column per asset. An asset is redundant when its column is a combination of the others.
Redundant assets $=$ assets $-$ rank. More assets than states forces at least one redundant asset.
A redundant asset is priced by its copy, by the law of one price. Any other market price is an arbitrage.

formula.name: Replication price
formula.note: Prices combine with the same weights as the payoff columns.

summary.trap: Redundant does not mean worthless. It means the asset can be copied, so its price is the copy's cost.

quiz.prose: Two states. A bond pays £100 in both and costs £96. A stock pays £50 or £150 and costs £98. A fund pays £150 or £250.
quiz.question: What is the fund's fair price?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the fund's payoffs as units of the bond and the stock.

byKey.payoff-avg: You averaged the fund's payoffs. Price its copy instead: one bond plus one stock.

explain.text: One bond plus one stock pays $100 + 50 = 150$ and $100 + 150 = 250$, the fund's payoffs. So the fund costs $96 + 98 = \text{£}194$.

options.text: At least one asset can be replicated from the others

options.why: Redundant assets still pay out. They are priced by their copy, not at zero.
A zero determinant only says one asset is redundant. Arbitrage needs a price that differs from the copy's cost.

feedback.correct: Dependent columns: some asset is a combination of the others.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A zero determinant is a statement about the payoff columns.

explain.text: $\det \mathbf{P} = 0$ means the columns are dependent, so some asset's payoff is a combination of the others. That asset is redundant and priced by replication.

quiz.prose: A redundant asset's copy costs £50.00, but the asset itself trades at £48.00.
quiz.question: Which trade locks in a riskless profit?

options.text: Buy the asset and sell the copy
Sell the asset and buy the copy
options.why: That sells the cheap side and buys the dear side: you pay £2 today for nothing later.

options.text: Buy the asset and hold it
options.why: Holding it alone leaves you exposed to the states. Selling the copy cancels every payoff.

feedback.correct: Buy cheap, sell dear: £2 today, nothing owed later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy whichever side is cheap and sell the other.

explain.text: Buy the asset for £48 and sell its copy for £50: you take in £2 today. The two payoffs cancel in every state, so the £2 is riskless.

quiz.prose: A market has 3 states and 5 assets.
quiz.question: At least how many assets are redundant?

feedback.correct: Rank at most 3, so at least $5 - 3 = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The rank cannot exceed the number of states.

byKey.zero: With only 3 states, the rank is at most 3, so 5 assets cannot all be independent.
byKey.three: 3 is the largest possible rank. The redundant count is $5 - 3$.

explain.text: A payoff matrix with 3 rows has rank at most 3. So at most 3 assets are independent, and at least $5 - 3 = 2$ are redundant.
